note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples for nine variants that hack2hire-chunk05-v1 had blocked. Inferred (mostly invented), not official. Examples are small inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

clarifyingQuestions: What are the two stability conditions exactly?
Must a stable segment contain at least one element strictly between its ends?
Can capacities be zero or negative?
hints: Write the condition with prefix sums: the middle sum is P[r] - P[l + 1].
For a fixed right end r you need left ends l <= r - 2 with capacity[l] == capacity[r] and P[l + 1] == P[r] - capacity[r].
Keep a hash map of (capacity[l], P[l + 1]) for l <= r - 2, inserting l = r - 2 just before processing r, and add the matching count.
invariants: before processing r the map holds exactly the left ends 0..r - 2
every counted pair has at least one element between its ends
chooseWhen: Counting subarrays defined by an equality on prefix sums
tradeoffs: The hash map makes the count linear; the quadratic double loop is simpler and fine for small n
hack2hire:68f82cd8d7ff180d0ab950c7.variantLabel: Single variant: count equal-ended segments whose ends equal their inner sum

constraints: times are "HH:MM" from 00:00 to 23:59, non-decreasing down the list
order ids are 1 to 10 letters or digits
every accepted order is finished later in the list
clarifyingQuestions: What is the base pay rate and its unit?
Is the rate multiplied by the number of ongoing orders or by something else?
Are there peak hours, and which?
How are cancelled orders paid?
In what unit is the total returned?
hints: Pay changes only when an order starts or finishes, so only row times matter.
Between two consecutive row times the number of ongoing orders is constant; multiply it by the paid minutes in between.
Keep a running count of ongoing orders and add 30 * count * gap at each row.
invariants: after processing a row, count equals the number of paid orders accepted and not yet finished
pay is accumulated in integer cents
chooseWhen: Piecewise-constant rate accumulation over a timeline
tradeoffs: The event sweep is linear in rows; the minute-by-minute simulation is simpler but costs 1440 times the number of orders
hack2hire:678472f60e1dbb6a09385781.variantLabel: Variant 1: base rate times concurrent orders

clarifyingQuestions: Which queries does the wrapper expose, and what do they return when no reading exists?
Can readings arrive out of timestamp order?
Is the average rounded, floored or returned as a fraction?
What exactly must be non-blocking: queries only, or recording too?
hints: Status 0 readings never affect any answer, so drop them at record time.
A windowed average needs the sum and the count of readings in a timestamp range; both are prefix-sum quantities.
With out-of-order arrivals, keep the sums in a Fenwick tree over timestamps; a hash map keeps it sparse.
invariants: the trees hold exactly the status-1 readings recorded so far
latest holds the maximum timestamp, the last-recorded one among ties
chooseWhen: Online range sums with point insertions in arbitrary key order
tradeoffs: A Fenwick tree answers both queries in O(log T); rescanning is simpler but linear per query. Neither addresses real thread safety
hack2hire:6a14a84c7b0582b352787d44.variantLabel: Single variant: latest and windowed average lux over valid readings

clarifyingQuestions: How is randomness made reproducible for testing (seed, injected deck)?
How is a round scored, and can it tie?
When does the game end and what is returned?
hints: Randomness only fixes the draw order; with the order given, the game is deterministic.
One round consumes two cards, so a pointer into the deck replaces removing cards.
Keep running scores so getScore and getWinner are O(1).
invariants: the pointer equals twice the number of rounds played
scores equal the sum of points of the rounds played so far
chooseWhen: Turn-based game simulation with deterministic replay
tradeoffs: Running scores give O(1) queries; replaying from the deck is simpler and self-checking but quadratic over a long trace
hack2hire:67842117d0faf7ec64cc3add.variantLabel: Variant 1: higher card wins one point per round

clarifyingQuestions: What does the second breaker guard: a secondary server, or a second failure measure on the same server?
After the cooldown, does one trial request decide, or several?
Is a request whose primary fails retried on the secondary?
What does a request return?
hints: Model one breaker as a tiny state machine: closed with a failure count, or open since some time.
An open breaker only needs its opening time; the cooldown check decides whether an attempt is a trial.
Write the breaker once and use two instances, primary first, falling back to the secondary.
invariants: a closed breaker's count equals its consecutive failures since the last success or opening
an open breaker never allows an attempt before opened + cooldown
chooseWhen: Fault-tolerance state machines driven by timestamps
tradeoffs: O(1) state per breaker; replaying histories is simpler to audit but quadratic
hack2hire:694609632c048134ada83559.variantLabel: Single variant: primary breaker with rerouting to a guarded secondary

constraints: 1 to 500 abusive words of 1 to 20 lowercase letters, at most 2000 letters in total
at most 60 substitution pairs, at most 3 letters per symbol
comment is at most 1e4 characters, tokens of 1 to 20 lowercase letters or symbols separated by single spaces
clarifyingQuestions: Is the substitution table given or fixed?
Can one symbol stand for several letters?
Do matches need whole tokens, or can they be substrings?
Return the flagged tokens, their positions, or a boolean?
hints: A token can only match words of its own length.
Put the words in a trie and walk it with the token.
A symbol can stand for several letters, so walk a set of trie nodes rather than one.
invariants: after reading i characters the set holds exactly the trie nodes whose prefix the first i characters can stand for
tradeoffs: The trie shares prefixes across words; the per-word scan is simpler and fine for few words
